Convert vectors for data preparation

Source: R/type-conversion.R
type_conversion.Rd

Prepare vectors using Stata-style conversion commands:

  • destring() (as_numeric()): Convert text to numbers; labelled numeric vectors use their stored values.

  • tostring() (as_character()): Convert stored values to text, using numeric codes for labelled numeric vectors and factors rather than labels.

  • encode(): Convert text categories to labelled integer codes, or retain a factor's integer codes with its levels as value labels.

  • decode(): Convert values to text, using value labels for labelled vectors and level text for factors.

Usage

destring(x, ignore = NULL)

decode(x)

encode(x)

tostring(x)

as_character(x)

as_numeric(x, ignore = NULL)

Arguments

x

A vector or matrix. For encode(), a character vector or factor without dimensions. Data frames are not accepted; convert their columns with dplyr::across().

ignore

NULL (default) or a single string of characters to remove from text before reading numbers, like Stata's ignore(). Each character is removed wherever it appears: ignore = "kg " removes k, g and spaces.

Value

Results retain the length and element order of x:

  • destring() (as_numeric()): A double vector. Invalid numeric text adds a problems attribute readable with readr::problems().

  • tostring() (as_character()): A character vector, except that character input is returned unchanged, including names, dimensions and attributes.

  • encode(): A haven_labelled integer vector with value labels and the input's variable label, if present. Names and other attributes are dropped.

  • decode(): A character vector containing value labels or converted values.

Except for the preservation rules above, names, dimensions, labels and units are dropped; matrices are flattened in column order. Empty inputs return typed empty results. None of these functions modifies the input.

Details

Reading numbers

destring() reads text the way Stata's destring does. A value must be a number, optionally with a sign, exponent, currency symbol (dollar, euro, pound, yen), thousands separators (1,234), a trailing percent sign (50% gives 50) and surrounding spaces, including non-breaking spaces. Anything else, such as "12abc", "10 kg" or a date, becomes NA with a warning, like Stata's force option; the positions and original values are kept in readr::problems(). Use ignore to remove other characters first, like Stata's ignore(): destring(x, ignore = "kg") reads "10 kg" as 10. Empty strings, "NA" and Stata's "." are missing without a warning; the text "NaN" becomes NaN. Date strings become NA; parse them with as.Date() or lubridate::ymd() instead.

A factor whose levels are all numbers, such as factor(c("1990", "2000")), gives those numbers (1990, 2000). Other factors give their level codes. Labelled numeric variables return their values; labelled text is read from its values like plain text. Unsupported numeric-conversion inputs, such as lists, raw vectors and complex vectors, return missing values of the same length.

Labels, missing values, and units

decode() uses value labels when a labelled vector has a nonempty labels attribute. Without value labels, it uses ordinary character conversion, including for tagged missing values, so 100000 gives "1e+05"; use tostring() to write numbers in full.

destring() and decode() keep SPSS user-missing codes as values or labels. Numeric conversion preserves tagged missing values. Dates become days since 1970-01-01; date-times become seconds since the Unix epoch. Durations and measured vectors retain their numeric values in their existing units. Conversion of large integer64 values to double can lose precision and emits the underlying conversion warning.

Encoding categories

encode() assigns codes 1, 2, 3, ... to distinct nonempty character values in UTF-8 radix order. Numeric-looking text is a category: "10", "20", "3" get codes 1, 2, 3, not the numbers 10, 20, 3. NA and "" become missing; spaces are retained. Radix ordering is reproducible but can differ from locale-specific alphabetical ordering in Stata.

For factors and ordered factors, encode() preserves the stored integer indices and uses all levels as value labels, including unused levels and explicit empty-string and NA levels. Numeric level text does not replace indices: factor(c(10, 20)) has codes 1 and 2. Ordering metadata is dropped.

encode(decode(x)) need not recover the original codes: decoding discards the dictionary, so re-encoding character text creates new codes starting at 1. Existing dictionaries cannot be supplied to encode(). Encode character columns before grouping to use one dictionary across groups; separate calls can assign conflicting codes. Factors with shared levels retain a common dictionary within grouped dplyr::mutate().

decode() follows Stata's value-label conversion but also accepts factors, labelled character vectors and unlabelled inputs as an R convenience. It falls back to ordinary character conversion when no value labels exist. For partial dictionaries, unlabelled values remain as text, whereas Stata returns empty strings for them.

Text formatting

tostring() and its alias as_character() ignore value labels: labelled numeric vectors and factors give their codes. For non-character input, values flagged by is.na(), including NaN, tagged missing values, and SPSS user-missing codes, become NA. Character input is returned unchanged. Numbers are written in full, so 100000 gives "100000", not "1e+05", with the significant digits of as.character() and a decimal point whatever options(OutDec) says. This precision policy can map distinct large numbers to the same text; keep identifiers as character or integer64 vectors when exact digits matter. AsIs wrappers are ignored for non-character input. Measured values and durations are written as numbers in their existing units. Dates use as.character(), giving "2024-01-31" rather than day numbers. Unlike Stata's tostring, missing values remain NA rather than becoming the strings "." or ".a" through ".z".

The sjlabelled package also exports as_numeric() and as_character(). They differ: sjlabelled's as_numeric() turns non-numeric text into factor codes, and its as_character() gives NA for unlabelled values. Whichever package is attached last masks the other; write tidystata::as_numeric() to be explicit, or use destring() and tostring(), which do not clash. To read value labels as text, use decode().

See also

Other conversion functions: na_conversion

Examples

lifeexp |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    region_chr = decode(region),
    region_code = tostring(region),
    region_num = destring(region),
    region_fct = haven::as_factor(region),
    .keep = "used"
  )
#> # A tibble: 68 × 5
#>    region               region_chr       region_code region_num region_fct      
#>    <dbl+lbl>            <chr>            <chr>            <dbl> <fct>           
#>  1 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  2 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  3 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  4 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  5 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  6 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  7 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  8 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#>  9 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#> 10 1 [Europe & C. Asia] Europe & C. Asia 1                    1 Europe & C. Asia
#> # ℹ 58 more rows

category <- encode(c("beta", "alpha", "beta", "", NA))
category
#> <labelled<integer>[5]>
#> [1]  2  1  2 NA NA
#> 
#> Labels:
#>  value label
#>      1 alpha
#>      2  beta
tostring(category) # integer codes as text
#> [1] "2" "1" "2" NA  NA 
decode(category) # category text
#> [1] "beta"  "alpha" "beta"  NA      NA     
encode(factor(c("Yes", "No"), levels = c("Unused", "No", "Yes")))
#> <labelled<integer>[2]>
#> [1] 3 2
#> 
#> Labels:
#>  value  label
#>      1 Unused
#>      2     No
#>      3    Yes
